blocks.text: Job 7 belongs to the long debate that follows seven days of silence from Job’s friends. Job speaks from anguish rather than hiding it, and the speeches that follow increasingly interpret his suffering as evidence of wrongdoing—an explanation Job rejects. The later conclusion of the book rebukes the friends, so their speeches should not be treated as undifferentiated guidance for responding to suffering.

Later readers connect Job with endurance and a compassionate outcome. In this setting, endurance need not mean silence: Job’s persistence includes his unrestrained lament and protest in chapters such as this one. It must not be used to demand that someone remain in abuse or forgo safety and protection.
